claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing structural alloys is primarily governed by grain-boundary chemical state.
High-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural alloys is primarily governed by grain-boundary chemical state.
Cohesion-enhancing dopant segregation suppresses dynamic grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures.
Cohesion-enhancing dopant segregation suppresses premature intergranular failure at elevated temperatures.
A minor addition of titanium or a similar grain-boundary-active element will preferentially segregate to grain boundaries.
The segregated dopant enhances grain-boundary cohesion by strengthening intergranular bonds.
Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion retards grain-boundary sliding.
Dopant-modified grain boundaries retard dynamic recrystallization.
Grain-boundary sliding is a dominant creep and strain-accommodation mechanism at high temperatures in the targeted alloys.
Reduced grain-boundary sliding increases overall toughness.
Reduced grain-boundary sliding delays the onset of plastic deformation.
The doped alloy will exhibit greater high-temperature ductility than the untreated baseline.
The doped alloy will exhibit greater high-temperature fracture toughness than the untreated baseline.
The doped alloy will have increased strain-to-failure relative to the baseline.
The doped alloy will show a delayed and more ductile failure mode relative to the baseline.
The hypothesis is expected to apply above 800°C when grain-boundary sliding contributes significantly to deformation.
The hypothesis requires an equiaxed microstructure, comparable grain sizes, and effective dopant-segregation kinetics at the test temperature.
